query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of coherent nanoprecipitations through stepwise thermo-mechanical processes can reduce post-exposure toughness degradation in high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.intervention: Stepwise thermo-mechanical processing to introduce coherent nanoprecipitations
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 25-800°C, duration: up to 50 hours, loading: uniaxial tensile tests
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces of the nanoprecipitations facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations, hindering dislocation motion and preventing premature crack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced post-exposure toughness degradation, maintaining ultrahigh strength and ductility
generation.boundary: Temperature: 25-800°C, duration: up to 50 hours, loading: uniaxial tensile tests
generation.uncertainty: The complexity of the alloy composition and the potential for incomplete peak deconvolution analysis may limit the accuracy of the predictions

falsification_experiment.design: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 800°C) on stepwise thermo-mechanically processed and untreated high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloys
measurements: Microstructural characterization via EBSD, TEM, STEM, and APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stepwise thermo-mechanically processed alloy exhibits significantly reduced toughness compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

System: (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (at.%) refractory high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase bcc/fcc structure. Processing: Arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 5 h, hot rolling at 1200 °C (80% reduction), cold rolling at 25 °C (75% reduction), annealing at 900 °C for 5 min, and aging at 650 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); microstructural characterization via EBSD, TEM, STEM, and APT.
